newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Samland plans onslaught on EU budget flaws.
newsitem.headline: Samland plans onslaught on EU budget flaws.

text.p: The head of the European Parliament's budget committee has ambitious plans to reform the European Union's spending habits between now and the next EP elections in June 1999.
Re-elected last week to lead the parliament's side of the bargaining with the Council of Ministers over the EU's annual budget, Detlev Samland has plenty to get his teeth into.
One of the most important decisions will be whether to raise the ceiling on EU spending after 1999, when the Union plans to expand into Central and East Europe.
European Commission President Jacques Santer is due at the end of 1997 to come up with proposals on the so-called financial perspectives for the early 21st century.

"I think we're in a situation where we could live with the (current spending limit) longer than 1999," Samland told Reuters in an interview, adding that a budget straightjacket was necessary for the success of the future single European currency.
"But that means either no (EU) enlargement or a change of policy," he said.

Since Samland, a German Socialist, is a fervent advocate of the EU's eastward expansion -- "for economic, political and peace-keeping reasons" -- the only other alternative he sees to inflating the EU budget is to curb farm subsidies and prune the costly Structural Funds.

Reform of the common agricultural policy (CAP), which absorbs some 45 percent of the EU annual 90-billion-Ecu budget, is inevitable anyway, Samland points out, because the EU committed itself during the Uruguay Round of world trade talks to axing farm subsidies by 30 percent by 1999.
Known for his debonaire style of dress, the former budget chief at Germany's largest television company, WDR, has a more austere approach when it comes to money.
Six months before work on the 1998 budget is due to begin, he has already proposed a root and branch reform of the system to the Dutch, who currently hold the presidency of the Council of Ministers.
He calls this "zero-based budgeting", or ditching all the compartments of the previous year's budget (the budget lines) and starting afresh.
"Zero-based budgeting means that every (EU subsidy) has to fight for itself. It will not exist just because it existed in the past," Samland warned.
EU ministers are happy to do this, he said, when it comes to spending on the EU's internal and external activities, over which the parliament has the final say.
But they are more reticent about "compulsory" farm spending, which is decided unilaterally by the Council.

The inter-governmental conference on reform of the EU treaty is looking as parliament's request for a joint say in all sections of the budget, including farming, though Samland is not optimistic that member states will agree.

Rows about democratic accountability apart, the current set- up is deeply unsatisfying to MEPs because the Council regularly overestimates the share of the EU's finite annual budget which it needs for agriculture, is unable to use all the money and ends up giving refunds to the member states.
Pending a decision on the farm budget, Samland will continue campaigning to stop the cycle of taxpayers' contributions- underspend-refund affecting the Structural and Social Funds.

Countries which are net contributors to the EU budget actually benefit from not using their allocations from these funds, which they have to match Ecu for Ecu from their national coffers, Samland pointed out.
"If they don't take EU money, they don't have to co-finance (projects) and they can get it back."
Germany, for example, was entitled to use 18 percent of the Structural Funds but could get 29 percent back in refunds, he said.
Samland may make swifter progress in resolving another of his committee's ongoing battles with the Council, over a question of principle rather than money.
Parliament is more than a little irked by what it sees as Britain's bad faith in dealing with aspects of EU social policy it does not like.

Britain is blocking the release of funds for several small- scale projects already approved by Council, including Education Commissioner Edith Cresson's plans for a youth voluntary service, because the decisions have not been enshrined in specific EU laws.

"On the other hand, they are the ones who block the legal base in Council," Samland complained. "It does not look very credible to European people when we can't do things because the money is there but the legal base is missing."

He hopes this year to persuade the Council to accept a compromise which would allow the European Commission to fund short one-off pilot projects costing under 10 million Ecus -- like the European Year against Racism -- with ministers' simple approval.
Bigger, longer-term programmes, such as EU aid schemes for refugees, will only be able to go ahead if they are backed up by a new EU law.

Over the next two years parliament's budget committee wants to work with Budget Commissioner Erkki Liikanen, for whom Samland has great respect, to cut wastage and anacronisms in the EU bodies' internal administration.
No new posts will be created in the Commission, the Council or the parliament this year or next.
And there will be pressure to end anomalies such as the long-standing tax exemption on petrol, alcohol and cigarettes which certain top grade officials are allowed.
"That's absolutely ridiculous. The reason at the time it was developed was that no one wanted to come to Brussels. Now 50,000 want to come when there's a call for 200!" Samland explained.
Staff pensions are another thing to have run out of control since the EU was created over 40 years ago.
The founders never thought about setting up a pension fund for their staff, whose retirement payments are drawn from the EU's general budget.
The problem is that by the time it comes to paying the pensions the EU has already spent the money elsewhere and the bill is expected to soar to over two billion Ecus.
Samland professes to be an optimist -- "Otherwise I wouldn't be here" -- and is looking forward to a more fruitful relationship with Council this year.
A breakthrough was made when the Dutch presidency of the Council agreed that for the next six months, the parliament could deal directly with EU finance ministers on budget matters.
Until now, parliament's interlocutors have been the national budget ministers, whom Samland describes as powerless paymasters with "no political vision and no political view".
He hopes this exception will become the rule: "It's the only way to make progress," he said.
